new_statements.rule_in_words: In the (polysynthetic) verb, primary stress falls on the first heavy syllable (long vowel or closed syllable, coda s counting) of the stem, i.e. the domain following the inflectional and instrumental prefixes, which are never stressed; by Talmy's account a stem with no heavy syllable would take final stress. Analysis rests on Talmy's 1972 verb data (speaker Selina LaMarr) and Talmy's unpublished phonological notes.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on alternating syllables on both sides of the primary-stressed syllable (attributed to Talmy's notes).
new_statements.exceptions: Instrumental prefixes never bear stress; coda s after a short vowel makes the syllable heavy for stress ([44]); the separate 'first-syllable heavy' restriction does not interact with stress ([53]). CONFLICTING EARLIER ANALYSIS: Olmsted 1958 (IJAL 24:219, sec. 4) treats stress as phonemic with three degrees (ordinary/strong/contrastive) and gives no positional rule; Olmsted 1961 (IJAL 27:91, sec. 2.2) says 'The one unpredictable aspect of the hortative is the place of stress', dividing verbs into endoaccentual (stress on the root) and exoaccentual (stress on final -ja:) classes, and (4.42) lists roots/affixes that 'always have the stress' -- i.e. lexical/morphological stress on Olmsted's Hat Creek data (speaker Ike Wilson).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the verb STEM (root + directional/derivational suffixes, excluding inflectional and instrumental prefixes) within the sentential verb word; all examples are inflected verb words from Talmy 1972 in broad-phonetic transcription. Nothing is said about nouns or citation forms of non-verbs. Source is a conference handout ('sketch'), explicitly preliminary and partly relaying Talmy p.c./notes.
new_statements.identity_note: Good 2004 analyses Talmy's 1965-70 data from Selina LaMarr (Atsugewi proper); Olmsted 1958/1961 describe the Hat Creek (Atsuge) dialect of Ike Wilson only and explicitly exclude the Apwaruge / Dixie Valley dialect. All refer to glottocode atsu1245 (no Glottolog dialect sub-codes used). Note the analytic conflict: Olmsted = phonemic/lexical stress (endo- vs exoaccentual verbs); Talmy/Good = predictable, weight-sensitive within the verb stem.

new_statements.relation_note: Differs in type, not placement: the Lexicon (following Olmsted 1958) treats stress as a phonemic property written on each word, with many words lacking strong stress, whereas the catalog's existing statement (Good 2004, from Talmy's verb data) derives stress by rule: never on instrumental prefixes, on the first heavy syllable of the stem, secondary stress alternating. The Lexicon gives no rule of its own and does not argue against a rule, so the disagreement is one of analytic stance (structuralist phonemic marking vs a predictable weight rule), and unmarked headwords such as aji, ahwi, ajqam are the concrete data that a first-heavy-syllable rule would have to account for. Weak evidence; fl…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The Lexicon states no placement rule. It says only that the transcription is phonemic and distinguishes two degrees of stress, ordinary (left unmarked) and strong (acute accent), and refers the reader to Olmsted 1958 for the analysis. Consistent with that, strong stress is written entry by entry on different syllables (ahwí 'tree', ajkuséna 'gizzard', ajtatí 'grayback', jusí· 'in') while many headwords carry no strong stress at all (aji 'water', ahwi 'wood', ajha 'lake', ajqam 'kidney'). The reading 'lexical (unpredictable)' is an inference from 'phonemic' plus per-entry marking, not a sentence in the book; 'none found' would be the reading if only explicit placement statements count.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. (Olmsted 1958 sec. 4, held by the project in the IJAL 24(3) text, adds a third 'contrastive' degree /ˋ/ that the Lexicon drops.)
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. The Preface notes that all recorded alternants (long vowel / short vowel / vowel + glottal stop, dialect mixture with Achumawi, age- and sex-graded variants) are listed as morphophonemic, not phonemic, alternations.
new_statements.identity_note: The Lexicon's data are 'mostly from the Hat Creek dialect' (Atsuge); forms marked AB come from Arthur Barnes, the single Apwaruge (Dixie Valley) informant. Its stress note is not dialect-specific. Good 2004's rule rests on Talmy's 1972 material (dialect not stated in the handout).

readall_conflicts: Olmsted's works and Good 2004 do not describe stress the same way. Olmsted 1958 (IJAL 24:219-220, sec. 4, held by the project) states 'Atsugewi has three phonemic degrees of stress: ordinary.. strong stress /ˊ/ and contrastive stress /ˋ/' and gives words with only ordinary stress (t?spa· 'bark', namistaq 'cloud') beside words with strong stress (táta 'father'); the 1984 Lexicon keeps two of those degrees, marks strong stress word by word, and leaves many entries unmarked. Good 2004 (the catalog's only statement) instead gives a predictable rule from Talmy's 1972 verb forms: instrumental prefixes never stressed, stress on the first heavy syllable of the stem, secondary stress on alternating syllables, with Talmy's remark that a stem with no heavy syllable would take final stress. The two are not reconciled anywhere in the sources opened; Good does not cite Olmsted's stress analysis. Since the Lexicon states no placement rule, the weight-sensitive rule stays the best-supported placement statement, but the catalog should note that the primary describer treated stress as phonemic.

sources.note: Sec. 2.2 (p. 91): 'The one unpredictable aspect of the hortative is the place of stress. Accordingly, verbs may be divided into two classes: endoaccentual (those which show the stress on some part of the root) and exoaccentual (those which show the stress on the final -ja:)'. Sec. 4.42: certain affixes/roots 'always have the stress', forms with more than one stress are 'not unusual'; stress 'only morphemically predictable'. I.e. lexical/morphological stress in Olmsted's analysis.
